title: How a MOSFET switches: gate charge, Rds(on), and thermal limits
summary: A linear read-through of MOSFET switching: gate charge moves the device, Rds(on) sets conduction loss, and heat decides whether it survives.

blocks.title: Charge the gate, then count the heat
blocks.body: A power MOSFET is a voltage-controlled switch. This page walks the story once, in order: what the gate charge does, why Rds(on) matters when the device is on, and how thermal limits close the loop. No sliders — just the causal chain.

blocks.heading: The three ideas, in reading order

nodes.title: 1. Gate charge
nodes.detail: You must move charge onto the gate before the channel fully enhances.

nodes.title: 2. Rds(on)
nodes.detail: Once on, the channel looks like a small resistance — I²R heat while conducting.

nodes.title: 3. Thermal limit
nodes.detail: Junction temperature rises until cooling balances loss, or the part fails.

blocks.heading: The gate is a capacitor you have to fill
blocks.body: Between gate and channel sits capacitance. To turn the FET on, a driver must supply gate charge Qg so Vgs climbs through the threshold and past the plateau where the drain voltage is swinging. Datasheets quote total gate charge and often break out Qgs, Qgd (the Miller charge), and Qgd-related switching energy. Slow gate drive stretches the time spent in the linear region, where voltage and current overlap and switching loss spikes.

items.label: Threshold — channel just begins to form
Vds falling/rising while Vgs hangs nearly flat
Total charge the driver must deliver each cycle

blocks.title: Driver current is not optional detail
blocks.body: If the gate resistor and driver cannot move Qg quickly, the FET spends extra time half-on. That shows up as heat even when Rds(on) looks excellent on paper.

blocks.heading: When it is on, it is a resistor
blocks.body: After the gate is charged and Vds has collapsed, conduction loss is roughly I_d² × Rds(on). Rds(on) is specified at a given Vgs and rises with junction temperature — a hot FET is a worse resistor. Choosing a part with half the Rds(on) halves conduction loss only if you actually drive the gate to the voltage the datasheet used for that rating.

blocks.caption: Numbers are teaching examples, not a design sign-off. Always include switching loss and temperature rise of Rds(on).

blocks.heading: Heat is the product of loss and thermal resistance
blocks.body: Junction temperature rises above ambient by P_total × RθJA (or a more detailed chain through case and heatsink). P_total is conduction loss plus switching loss plus any diode recovery contribution. The datasheet's absolute maximum T_j is a cliff, not a target — reliable designs keep margin, derate with ambient, and remember that Rds(on) itself climbs as the die heats, which can run away if cooling is marginal.

blocks.heading: A linear check before you ship a board
items: Confirm the gate driver can deliver Qg in the time your switching frequency allows.
Estimate conduction loss from expected current and hot Rds(on), not only 25°C numbers.
Add switching loss from datasheets or scope measurements of V×I overlap.
Translate total watts through the thermal stack and confirm T_j stays inside your derating plan.

columns.name: Slow gate / high f_sw
columns.detail: Switching loss and Miller-region time dominate. Fix drive strength and layout inductance first.

columns.name: High current, modest f_sw
columns.detail: Conduction loss dominates. Chase Rds(on), copper, and cooling.

columns.name: Tight enclosure
columns.detail: Thermal resistance dominates even moderate watts. Airflow and heatsinking decide survival.

blocks.heading: Causal check
blocks.prompt: A FET runs cool at low PWM frequency but overheats when you raise frequency, even though average load current is unchanged. What is the most likely first suspect?
options: Rds(on) suddenly doubled because of the frequency change alone
Switching loss rose with more transitions per second while conduction loss stayed similar
The gate charge disappeared from the datasheet
blocks.explanation: More switching events per second increase switching energy per unit time. Conduction loss tracks current and Rds(on), which did not change in the prompt.
blocks.correctFeedback: Yes — frequency scales switching loss when each transition still costs energy.
blocks.wrongFeedback: Re-read Sections 1 and 3. Frequency multiplies switching events; Rds(on) does not jump just because PWM got faster.

blocks.quote: Charge the gate cleanly, respect the ohms when it is on, and give the heat somewhere to go.
